content: There are several doctorate-level degrees in nursing, including the Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP or DrNP), the Doctor of Nursing Science (DNSc, DNS, or DSN), and the Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in Nursing. The Doctor of Nursing (ND) degree has been discontinued, and most universities have transitioned to offering the DNP instead. The PhD and DNS degrees are generally considered research-oriented, while the DNP is a practice-oriented or clinical doctorate. The Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP or DrNP) is an advanced-level practice degree that emphasizes the clinical aspects of nursing rather than academic research. The curriculum for the DNP typically includes advanced practice, leadership, and the application of clinical research in nursing. The primary goal of the DNP is to prepare registered nurses (RNs) to become advanced practice nurses. Advanced practice roles in nursing include Nurse Practitioners (NPs), Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists (CRNAs), Certified Nurse Midwives (CNMs), and Clinical Nurse Specialists (CNSs). Many other professions, such as medicine, dentistry, and pharmacy, require entry-level professional doctorates for practice. Similarly, the DNP was developed in response to changes in healthcare delivery and emerging healthcare needs, as well as the increasing complexity of knowledge required for leadership in nursing. The American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) has mandated that all entry-level nurse practitioner programs transition from the Master of Science in Nursing (MSN) to the DNP by 2015. Similarly, the American Association of Nurse Anesthetists has required the DNP (or DNAP, Doctor of Nurse Anesthesia Practice) for entry-level nurse anesthetist programs by 2025. However, nurse practitioners and nurse anesthetists currently practicing with an MSN will not be required to obtain the DNP. The Doctor of Nursing Science (DNSc, DNS, or DSN) is a professional-level research degree in nursing, while the Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in Nursing is an academic degree designed to prepare candidates for research and teaching positions. When the DNSc was first introduced in the 1970s, it was intended to be a clinical or practice-based doctorate. However, the DNSc curriculum was found to be very similar to the research-based PhD program. The DNSc requires the completion of a dissertation or a substantial project for graduation. With the introduction of the DNP as a clinical-oriented degree, some nursing schools have begun phasing out DNSc programs. For example, Yale University and Rush University, which previously offered the DNSc, now only offer the PhD in Nursing.
